topic.subject: science
topic.title: Work and energy
topic.scope: work in physics, kinetic and potential energy, conservation of energy, power, commercial unit of energy

misconceptions.statement: If I push a heavy wall until I am exhausted, I have done a lot of work.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse biological effort and fatigue with the physics definition of work.
misconceptions.fix: In physics, work is only done when a force causes a displacement; if the wall doesn't move, work is zero.

probe.question: A student pushes a stationary truck for 1 hour but it doesn't budge. How much work is done?
probe.wrong_answer: A large amount of work because the student is tired.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: A coolie carrying a suitcase on his head while walking horizontally is doing work on the suitcase.
misconceptions.why: Students see movement and force and assume work must be happening.
misconceptions.fix: Work is zero when the force (upward) is perpendicular to the displacement (horizontal).

probe.question: A person holds a 10kg box and walks 5m on a level floor. What is the work done by the lifting force?

misconceptions.statement: If the speed of a car doubles, its kinetic energy also doubles.
misconceptions.why: Students often assume linear relationships between variables.
misconceptions.fix: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity, so doubling speed quadruples the energy.

probe.question: A car's speed increases from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its KE change?

misconceptions.statement: Potential energy depends on the path taken to reach a certain height.
misconceptions.why: Students think a longer path (like a ramp) requires more energy to overcome.
misconceptions.fix: Gravitational potential energy depends only on the vertical height difference, not the path taken.

probe.question: Object A is lifted vertically 2m. Object B is pushed up a 5m ramp to the same 2m height. Which has more PE?
probe.wrong_answer: Object B because the path is longer.

misconceptions.root_belief: the process determines the final state

misconceptions.statement: When a moving ball comes to a stop on the floor, its energy is destroyed.
misconceptions.why: Students cannot see the heat or sound energy, so they assume the energy vanished.
misconceptions.fix: Energy is never destroyed; it transforms into other forms like heat due to friction and sound.

probe.question: A rolling ball stops due to friction. Where did its kinetic energy go?
probe.wrong_answer: It was used up and now it is gone.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: A person who finishes a job faster has done more work than a slower person.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the rate of doing work (power) with the total amount of work.
misconceptions.fix: Work depends only on force and displacement; time only affects the power.

probe.question: Anil climbs stairs in 10s. Sunil climbs the same stairs in 20s. Who did more work?

misconceptions.statement: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of power.
misconceptions.why: The presence of the word 'watt' leads students to associate it with power.
misconceptions.fix: kWh is a unit of energy (Power x Time), used for commercial electricity billing.

probe.question: Your electricity bill says you used 50 units (kWh). What physical quantity is this?

misconceptions.statement: Only living things or machines have energy.
misconceptions.why: Students associate energy with the ability to move or 'life force'.
misconceptions.fix: All objects, living or non-living, can possess energy based on their motion or position.

probe.question: Does a non-living rock sitting on a cliff have energy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not alive and not moving.

misconceptions.statement: An object on the ground has zero potential energy.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the ground as an absolute zero for energy.
misconceptions.fix: Potential energy is relative; an object on the ground still has PE relative to a basement or a pit.

probe.question: If we dig a hole next to a ball on the ground, does the ball's potential energy change relative to the hole?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is zero because it is on the ground.

misconceptions.statement: Work cannot be negative because it is not a vector.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the scalar nature of work with the inability to have a negative value.
misconceptions.fix: Work is a scalar, but it can be negative if the force and displacement are in opposite directions.

probe.question: What is the sign of work done by friction on a sliding block?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive, because work is a scalar.

misconceptions.why: Language like 'generating power' or 'producing energy' suggests creation from nothing.
misconceptions.fix: Batteries and fuels only transform stored chemical energy into other forms like electrical or heat energy.

probe.question: Where does the energy in a battery come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The battery creates it when you turn it on.

misconceptions.statement: A more powerful engine always does more work than a less powerful one.
misconceptions.fix: A more powerful engine does work faster, but a less powerful engine can do more total work if it runs for a longer time.

probe.question: Engine A (100W) runs for 1 hour. Engine B (500W) runs for 1 minute. Which did more work?
probe.wrong_answer: Engine B because it is more powerful.

misconceptions.root_belief: strength and power are the same
